paper_title: LynnReal-Hand: Unlocking World Interaction with Hand Control

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Interactive video world models enable exploration through text and camera controls, yet direct object interaction requires finer control. Hands provide a natural interface, but translating continuous hand movements into coherent visual responses remains challenging because of complex hand-object dynamics and demanding real-time computation. To address these challenges, we introduce LynnReal-Hand, a hand-controlled video world model that unifies precise interaction modeling with efficient streaming generation. We curate 100K interaction clips spanning diverse real and synthetic environments and develop hand-aware supervision to improve fine-grained hand motions and object interactions. Building on this foundation, we learn a causal flow map for few-step generation and introduce region-aware score distillation that combines complementary video and image priors to refine interaction dynamics and visual appearance. To further reduce inference latency, we propose Ultra-Fast-VAE, a compact video decoder that preserves high reconstruction fidelity with substantially lower computational cost. Extensive evaluations on HandBench demonstrate superior hand-following accuracy and visual quality compared with existing approaches. Our full-sequence model achieves an FVD of 181.67 and a MANO Dice score of 93.02, while the three-step causal model maintains a MANO Dice score of 92.49. For real-time interaction, 540p streaming on a single H200 reaches 18.03 FPS with 741ms latency and an optimized peak GPU memory footprint of only 34.89GB. We will release the datasets, model weights, and the full training and inference code to support research on hand-controlled video world models.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Interactive video world models are transforming video generation from passive content synthesis into environments that respond to user actions. Early systems such as Genie [1] demonstrated action-controllable generation, while recent advances in Matrix-Game 3.0 [2], PAN [3], and open world models [47] have improved interactivity, temporal consistency, and accessibility. Yet most interaction paradigms remain centered on navigation, camera motion, or high-level instructions. These controls determine where users look or move, but offer limited ability to manipulate the objects they encounter. Enabling such manipulation requires world model to respond not only to changes in viewpoint, but also to the fine-grained actions through which users interact with their surroundings. Hands offer direct and expressive interface for this purpose: reaching, grasping, releasing, and coordinated bimanual movements communicate intentions that are difficult to specify through text or navigation commands. Recent efforts, including HandWorld [8], Hand2World [9], Generated Reality [10], Dexterous World Models [11], and JointControlVideo [12], have begun to connect articulated hand motion with visual generation. However, reliable hand-controlled interaction presents challenges that are distinct from conventional video synthesis. First, hands and their contact regions occupy only small portion of each frame, so global generative objectives can underemphasize precisely the details that determine control fidelity. Second, accelerating high-quality video model into few-step causal generator can amplify local motion errors: the student must preserve articulated interactions while conditioning on its own imperfect history. Finally, even when denoising is accelerated, decoding high-resolution video latents can remain major obstacle to responsive interaction. These challenges call for training and inference pipeline that preserves interaction fidelity throughout the transition from full-sequence learning to streaming generation. We introduce LynnReal-Hand, an open-source hand-controlled video world model developed to address these challenges end to end. At its core is Interaction-Preserving Training (IPT), supervision strategy that explicitly prioritizes fine-grained interaction fidelity at two critical stages: full-sequence pretraining and causal distribution matching. We first build dataset of 100K interaction clips with aligned hand trajectories, camera poses, and textual descriptions across diverse real and synthetic scenes. During full-sequence learning, we go beyond global flow matching with hand-aware multilevel supervision: handregion latent objective penalizes local reconstruction errors directly, while decoded LPIPS and DINOv2 constraints reinforce perceptual structure and hand appearance. This targeted supervision counteracts the weak contribution of small interaction regions to the global training signal and establishes stronger teacher for subsequent acceleration. Building on this pretrained model, we learn causal flow map [13] that generates each video chunk in only three denoising transitions. Teacher-forced training with clean history provides an efficient initialization, but leaves mismatch with inference, where each new chunk depends on previously generated content. We therefore refine the causal student on self-generated rollouts using distribution matching [14, 15]. However, global score matching alone does not distinguish the visual evidence needed for interaction dynamics from the evidence needed for scene appearance. To allocate these complementary signals, we formulate region-aware dual-score distillation: hand-conditioned video teacher and critic guide the entire generated sequence, with higher-noise evaluations emphasizing interaction-related corrections, while complementary image prior supplies appearance guidance only outside hand regions. This spatial separation is essential because the image prior lacks hand conditions and should not override the specified motion. In this way, IPT addresses complementary failure modes of the two training stages: insufficient hand-local learning during pretraining and degraded interaction fidelity during causal acceleration. For open-ended streaming, bounded attention window and local temporal-position reset keep the students history and positional range finite. Efficient generation also requires efficient reconstruction. We therefore introduce Ultra-Fast-VAE, compact Transformer decoder that preserves the generators native latent interface while compressing attention and feed-forward branches and recovering reconstruction quality through representation and temporal distillation. We evaluate the resulting system with HandBench, covering ten hand-interaction sources, including two held-out sources for out-of-distribution testing. On the main benchmark, LynnReal-HandBase achieves an FVD of 181.67 and MANO Dice score of 93.02; the evaluated LynnReal-Hand-Fast model, trained with video-score distillation but without the image-guidance branch, retains 92.49 MANO Dice with three denoising steps. In separate optimized 540p streaming evaluation on one H200, Fast reaches 18.03 FPS. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: 2 Interaction-scale data and evaluation. We curate 100K hand-interaction clips with temporally aligned hand, camera, and semantic conditions, and establish HandBench to assess control fidelity and visual quality across diverse scenes and held-out settings. Interaction-Preserving Training. We develop unified supervision perspective spanning hand-aware multilevel learning for full-sequence generation and region-aware score allocation for causal distillation, explicitly addressing how hand-control signals are preserved at both stages. Few-step, open-ended causal generation. We combine causal flow-map learning, refinement on self-generated histories, and bounded-window temporal-position management to support three-step streaming generation without an ever-growing attention cache. Fast, high-fidelity video decoding. We propose Ultra-Fast-VAE, which compresses pretrained Transformer decoder while retaining its native latent interface and restoring spatial and temporal reconstruction fidelity through targeted distillation.

sections.title: 2.1 Interactive Video World Models
sections.content: Video world models use learned visual prediction to make an environment respond to user inputs. Genie [1], Matrix-Game 3.0 [2], and PAN [3] develop action-based interaction and long-horizon simulation. WorldPlay [4] and RELIC [5] study geometric consistency and memory, while LingBot-World [6] and SolarWM [7] advance open training and deployment. BiWM [16] provides an open training framework for bidirectional autoregressive world models. These advances provide foundation for interactive synthesis. Our focus is the additional control and supervision needed when user specifies articulated hand motion within the generated scene.

sections.title: 2.2 Hand-Controlled Video Generation
sections.content: Hand-conditioned generation represents actions using meshes, joints, or other spatial controls. HandWorld [8] jointly models video and hand actions; Hand2World [9] studies hand-driven interaction; and Generated Reality [10] combines hand and camera conditioning. Dexterous World Models [11] grounds interaction in rendered static scenes and hand trajectories, while DexAC [17], P3-WAM [18], and JointControlVideo [12] study complementary structured action representations. DreamDojo [19] and EgoWM [20] further connect action-conditioned prediction with embodied learning. We build on this problem setting and study its full training-to-delivery path. In particular, our method emphasizes local hand supervision, separates temporal and appearance score gradients during causal distillation, and reduces the codec cost. Section 5 compares the available native model paths under their recorded conditions.

sections.title: 2.3 Efficient Generation and Open Recipes
sections.content: Few-step generation reduces the repeated computation of diffusion sampling. AnyFlow [13] learns finite flow transitions; DMD [14] estimates distribution-matching updates from real and fake scores; and Self-Forcing [15] trains autoregressive generators on their own histories. PackForcing [21] bounds long-video history through partitioned KV caches, compression, and context selection. DuoMatching [22] combines video-joint and image-marginal supervision. For hand control, these objectives must preserve small, moving interaction region as well as global visual appearance. Our score separation assigns these responsibilities explicitly. We also address the complementary rendering cost: Ultra-Fast-VAE retains the native generator latent interface and reconstructs each completed chunk with narrower attention and feed-forward branches, connecting denoising acceleration to measured reconstructionlatency trade-off.

High-fidelity Transformerbased VAE decoders incur substantial computational overhead, even with recent streaming optimizations [32, 33]. Lightweight CNN alternatives offer lower latency but often sacrifice fine-grained reconstruction quality [34], particularly for articulated hands and manipulated objects. sections.title: 3.6 Data Engine Construction
sections.content: We construct unified data pipeline for handand camera-conditioned egocentric video generation. The pipeline converts heterogeneous videos into interaction clips with temporally aligned 3D hand parameters, hand renderings, camera trajectories, and textual descriptions. It combines visual quality filtering, motion annotation, interaction verification, and diversity-aware sampling to obtain training corpus of 100K clips. Video collection and preprocessing. We collect videos from public egocentric datasets and online sources, supplemented with first-person interaction videos synthesized by MiniMax-H3 [26]. Source videos must have resolution of at least 720p, frame rate of at least 24 fps, and more than 200 frames; only egocentric views are retained from multiview recordings. We use OmniShotCut [37] to identify shot boundaries and exclude transition intervals. Within each continuous shot, we extract 125or 240-frame clips at 24 fps. To provide sharp conditioning image, we select the starting frame with the highest grayscale Laplacian variance among up to ten valid frames following each candidate cut position. Clips are encoded as H.264 videos with 768-pixel short side while preserving aspect ratio. We additionally enhance subset of videos using SparkVSR to improve visual quality. We reject poorly exposed clips using brightness statistics, then retain the top 80% 8 ranked by the overall COVER quality score [38]. PaddleOCR detects persistent subtitles in the lower third of the image. Subtitled landscape clips are discarded; portrait clips are consistently cropped only when subtitle removal requires trimming at most 25% of the image height. All cropping precedes motion annotation. Hand annotation and detection completion. We apply the WiLoR hand detector [39] frame by frame, remove duplicate and temporally inconsistent detections, and discard clips with hands detected in fewer than 50% of frames. For retained clips, short gaps bounded by valid same-side detections are filled by interpolating box centers and sizes when the preceding hand is away from the image boundary. Remaining gaps are addressed with SAM 3 [40], prompted with hand within an enlarged region around the preceding same-side box. We convert the largest predicted instance into box, preserve the tracks handedness, and limit consecutive SAM-based completions. After further cleanup and smoothing, clips with hand coverage below 90% are rejected. WiLoR then estimates MANO [41] pose, shape, global orientation, and camera-space translation from the completed boxes. We temporally smooth parameters within valid intervals and render the resulting meshes on black background, matching the video clips frame count, resolution, and frame rate. Camera annotation. We estimate camera intrinsics and per-frame poses with ViPE [42], using GeoCalib for intrinsic initialization and MoGe-2 metric depth priors to constrain scale during geometric optimization. To reduce interference from moving hands, we extract binary silhouettes from the hand renderings, apply morphological closing and dilation, and exclude these regions from the geometric constraints. Reusing hand annotations replaces ViPEs generic foreground detection and segmentation stages. We reject trajectories with missing or invalid poses, inconsistent frame indexing, translation jumps, abrupt rotations, or repeated large direction reversals. Translation steps exceeding five times the local mean, adjacent rotations above 60, and relative rotations above 100 within approximately 1.2 seconds trigger rejection. Semantic annotation and interaction verification. We use Qwen3.8-Flash-Next [43], deployed with vLLM, to assign background and activity labels and generate interaction descriptions from chronologically ordered frames sampled at 1 Hz, including the first frame. Descriptions establish the initial scene and summarize visible actions and state changes without inventing unobserved events. Camera motion and viewpoint changes are excluded from the text, leaving them to the camera condition. In separate verification pass, the model examines frames sampled every 25 frames and checks three criteria: an egocentric viewpoint, only the camera wearers hands with no other people visible, and purposeful handobject interaction. We retain only clips that explicitly pass all three checks. Valid interactions include grasping, placing, assembly, tool use, and sustained manipulation; hovering, empty gestures, and static display are excluded. Training-set selection. Finally, we sample without replacement using weights proportional to the product of inverse background-label and activity-label frequencies. This increases the selection probability of less frequent environments and actions. Each selected sample contains video clip, aligned hand parameters and renderings, camera intrinsics and poses, and an interaction caption, providing visual targets and complementary motion and language conditions for generation training.

sections.title: 4.1 Benchmark Construction
sections.content: Evaluating hand-controlled video generation requires assessing not only visual realism but also whether the generated interactions faithfully follow the specified hand motions. Existing video quality metrics alone cannot adequately capture such fine-grained control accuracy, particularly for complex hand-object interactions. To enable more comprehensive evaluation, we construct HandBench, benchmark that jointly assesses hand-motion fidelity, visual quality, and scene consistency across diverse interaction scenarios. HandBench comprises 200 video sequences collected from ten sources, with 20 sequences each from EgoDex [44], H2O [45], HOI-4D [46], OpenAoE [47], TACO [48], ARCTIC [49], CaptainCook4D [50], Ego4D [51], EPIC-KITCHENS-100 [52], and synthetic scenes generated by H3 [26]. These sequences encompass diverse interaction patterns, including fine-grained object manipulation, coordinated bimanual actions, tool use, and interactions with articulated or deformable objects. For each sequence, we preserve the original video 9 interval, spatial crop, and temporally aligned hand and camera conditions to ensure consistent reference-based evaluation. We use 160 sequences from eight sources for the main benchmark. H2O and TACO are excluded from world-model training and reserved for out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluation, with 20 sequences from each source.

sections.title: 4.2 Evaluation Metrics and Protocol
sections.content: A reliable evaluation of hand-controlled generation must distinguish accurate motion following from visual plausibility, as realistic-looking videos may still deviate substantially from the prescribed hand trajectories. We therefore adopt projected MANO [41] mesh-silhouette Dice as our primary control metric, measuring the spatial agreement between reference hand geometry and hands independently reconstructed from generated frames. This metric evaluates whether the generated hand configurations follow the intended movements while accounting for their projected positions and shapes. To complement control accuracy, we evaluate reconstruction fidelity using PSNR, SSIM [53], and LPIPS [24], and assess video distribution quality using FVD [54]. We further measure semantic alignment and temporal consistency through weighted CLIP [55] similarity and VBench [56] subject and background consistency metrics. Camera-motion adherence is evaluated using background motion agreement, allowing us to distinguish viewpoint following from hand articulation. Together, these metrics provide complementary assessments of interaction fidelity and visual coherence without reducing them to single aggregate score. For fair comparison, we preserve each methods native temporal sampling and align generated frames with their corresponding reference frames. All methods are evaluated on common valid support, with scalar metrics aggregated using equal weights across data sources and FVD computed from pooled video features. sections.title: 6 Limitations and Future Work
sections.content: While LynnReal-Hand demonstrates promising performance in hand-controlled video generation, several directions remain open for further exploration. First, our current causal model operates with limited temporal context and does not explicitly model long-term memory, which may constrain interaction consistency over extended horizons. Incorporating persistent memory mechanisms could enable more coherent and continuous interactions in long-running virtual environments. Second, we observe that the causal flow-map model learned in Stage II already exhibits promising generation quality within the training sequence lengths, even before subsequent score distillation. This suggests an interesting direction toward directly learning high-quality fewstep generators through flow-map objectives, potentially eliminating the need for computationally expensive DMD training. We leave the exploration of these directions to future work.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduce LynnReal-Hand for continuous visual interaction through natural hand motion. Hand-aware supervision, few-step causal generation, and Ultra-Fast-VAE combine accurate control, high visual fidelity, and efficient decoding. Experiments across diverse interaction scenarios support the effectiveness of this framework.

sections.title: B Training and Implementation Details
sections.content: B.1 Stage-I Implementation The full 33B transformer is optimized in BF16 with frozen condition encoders and FlashAttention-3 [60]. Qwen encodes only the first image and caption; the native H3 VAE encodes the hand video. Native hand and target planes contain 24 42 tokens with 1 2 2 patches. Camera conditions use fixed intrinsics and first-relative extrinsics. H3s data-directed prediction has the opposite sign to the noise-directed velocity in the main text, with = 1 σ. All target planes are noised and supervised. Anchor and hand tensors use 0.999X + 0.001ϵ with time label 0.999. Hand perceptual supervision samples 16 16 latent crop, decodes five predicted latents with two detached context latents, and evaluates LPIPS and DINOv2 on the corresponding 256 256 hand region. The ROI margin is 0.2. B.2 Stage-II Implementation Stage II trains rank-384 LoRA [30] and interval-conditioning parameters (2.08B trainable parameters). FP32 AdamW uses (β1, β2) = (0.9, 0.95), cosine decay, and EMA 0.999; CFG is disabled. For the derivative term in Eq. 5, let = sg(vθ), σ = max(r, σ h), and σ+ = min(1, σ + h). We use (cid:20) U+ σ+ σ bDσU = sg (cid:21) , (21) = Uθ(z + (σ σ)d, σ, r). Target evaluations share conditions and are detached; only the interval prediction receives gradients. Interior time pairs apply the same monotone shift to and vu, for independent uniform u, v. Stopped loss balancing scales the interval objective relative to the diagonal reference. B.3 Stage-III Score Distillation The image bridge maps five 24-channel H3 planes through width-256 projection, eight spatial residual blocks, and 2 pixel-shuffle upsampling. Physical-offset embeddings select the corresponding frame. The bridge is frozen after fitting, while its input derivative remains active. Four temporal locations supply image supervision. Qwen-Image [31] uses CFG4 and native norm rescaling without hand or camera conditions; Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B [61] critic fits one-frame image latents. After the bridge VJP, image gradients are zeroed inside the hand ROI. The dual-score configuration uses video CFG3, shift-3 student rollout, and shift-12 video-score noise. The negative branch retains image and camera conditions while omitting hand and text conditions. Critics receive five optimizer updates per generator update after 10 warmup updates; the image weight ramps from 0.001 to 0.1 during warmup. Student EMA is 0.999. Earlier generated histories are detached when replaying trainable rollout exits. The evaluated Fast model uses video-score training with uniform noise, paired hand supervision, and non-hand adversarial term; its image-score branch and image critic are disabled.

sections.title: C Inference and Runtime
sections.content: C.1 Evaluated Model Paths LynnReal-Hand-Base uses joint CFG3 and the native H3 VAE at 1344 768. Its 30-point shift-3 schedule performs 29 Euler updates with two evaluations per update. Fast uses three shift-3 flow-map transitions, W2 history, native H3 anchor encoding, Tiny-H3 [34] hand encoding, and FP16 Ultra-Fast-VAE for quality evaluation. The same Fast model supplies the pairwise preference results. Streaming Hand2World [9] and JointControlVideo [12] use released models. Bidirectional Hand2World adapts rank-256 attention LoRA and its camera adapter on the adaptation corpus (84,305 examples; 32,000 sample visits), retaining 50 native sampling steps, CFG1, and the full Wan VAE without TeaCache [62]. 23 Generated Reality [10] adapts rank-32 LoRA and motion encoder in the official 5B model on 1,146 ARCTIC clips from subjects s01s09, reserving s10 for reproduction validation. All methods retain native source-frame alignment without frame repetition or playback changes. Schedule-specific AdaLN storage. For both LynnReal-Hand-Base and LynnReal-Hand-Fast, per-block AdaLN modulation depends only on the prescribed time conditions. fixed sampling schedule therefore needs only the modulation values at its visited times and clean-conditioning boundaries; Fast uses the corresponding start/end-time pairs. The inference export stores these values directly and omits the learned block projection matrices, avoiding their loading and device residency. The default Base and three-step Fast tables occupy 535.3 and 55.4 MiB, respectively. This storage specialization leaves the sampling rule unchanged; total memory also includes activations, codecs, KV caches, and graph buffers. C.2 Timing Boundaries and Hardware Table 2 reports single-H200 measurements. Baseline and Base rows use their available support from the original 140-clip timing cohort; different case support and resolutions preclude controlled speed ranking. Offline latency measures the full sequence. Streaming Hand2World reports native four-frame latency and post-anchor throughput. Comparison encoding is excluded. Base retains cached conditions and transformer/VAE device swaps with the native decoder; its peak uses the original full AdaLN projections. C.3 Optimized Streaming Deployment The accelerated Fast path combines quantized projections, fused operators, condition caches, full 50-block DiT compilation, CUDA graphs, and W8A8 Ultra-Fast-VAE on one H200. Native 960 544 computation is vertically cropped to 960 540 output. Three transitions and W2 history are retained. One warmup rollout and three measured repeats on the 124-frame example give 15 steady full chunks, yielding 18.0295 FPS and mean latency 740.69 ms. Latency starts with available hand/camera conditions and ends when synchronized frames reach host memory; it includes online hand encoding, prefill, generation, and decoding. Continuous FPS additionally includes the preceding clean KV commit. Loading, initial-image conditioning, cold compilation, warmup, video encoding, acquisition, and display are excluded. The Fast peak in Table 2 comes from separate measurement of the released sampling-specialized model on the same 124-frame input geometry. After one full warmup and release of unused allocator cache, three rollouts reach 34.89 GiB maximum PyTorch-allocated device memory. Conditions are prepared in advance, with the native H3 VAE and Qwen encoder off device during generation. The peak includes the quantized transformer, online hand encoder, Ultra-Fast-VAE, KV caches, and graph buffers; cold loading and conditioning preparation are excluded. Timing and the 768p quality evaluation use separate model weights and protocols.
